Pedro II of Brazil. Known as Dom Pedro II, he was the second and last emperor of Brazil who reigned for fifty-eight years, making him one of South America's longest-serving rulers. An educated, progressive monarch who modernized Brazil and avoided military authoritarianism, he was ultimately unable to prevent the abolition of slavery and the transition to a republic.

Pedro became emperor at age five following his father's abdication, and he ruled as a constitutional monarch until 1889. During his reign, he presided over Brazil's economic and cultural development, attracting European immigration, building railroads, and establishing schools and libraries. He abolished the slave trade in 1850 and gradually emancipated enslaved people. In 1888, a month before his abdication, he issued the Golden Law, ending slavery entirely. Faced with mounting pressure from republicans and a military coup in 1889, Pedro accepted exile to Europe without violent resistance. He died in exile in Paris in 1891. Though the Brazilian republic continued without him, he remains a respected figure in history, remembered for his intelligence, his science-minded interests, and his personal modesty despite holding absolute imperial power.
